content: The Guideline Development Group (GDG) recognized that it was not feasible to account for all potential confounding factors when comparing the 6-month (H)REZ regimen to longer (H)REZ regimens. For instance, although data on the extent of disease were not systematically collected for all patients, it is possible that a higher proportion of cases with extensive disease were treated with regimens longer than 6 months, which could have led to poorer outcomes in this group due to the severity of their disease. This may have inadvertently favored the 6-month regimen in outcome comparisons. The GDG acknowledged the safety concerns associated with the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen, particularly the risk of hepatotoxicity linked to prolonged use of pyrazinamide-containing multidrug regimens. However, reducing the duration of pyrazinamide treatment to 3 months or less was associated with worse treatment outcomes, especially in Hr-TB regimens that did not include a fluoroquinolone. Additionally, the use of streptomycin in these regimens did not provide any significant added benefit. The GDG noted that patients are likely to value a 6-month regimen highly due to the increased likelihood of achieving a relapse-free successful outcome and the preference for a regimen that does not require injectable agents. Members of the GDG agreed that the use of the 6-month (H)REZ regimen would likely enhance health equity, given the relatively low cost of its components compared to the recommended regimens for MDR/RR-TB. Furthermore, the exclusion of streptomycin and other injectable agents reduces potential barriers to regimen administration. Although patient costs were not explicitly considered in the analysis, the GDG emphasized the importance of improving diagnostic capacity to detect isoniazid resistance. A modeling analysis conducted for the 2011 update of the WHO Guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant tuberculosis estimated that performing drug susceptibility testing (DST) for all patients before treatment using a rapid test that detects resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin was the most effective strategy for preventing deaths and acquired MDR-TB. This modeling also demonstrated that rapid testing for resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin at the time of diagnosis was the most cost-effective testing strategy across all patient groups and settings, even in areas with low levels of resistance among TB patients. The GDG considered the 6-month (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen to be feasible in most DR-TB treatment settings. The use of an all-oral regimen may further enhance feasibility. Based on the available evidence, the GDG reached a consensus on the beneficial effects of the Hr-TB regimen when used in accordance with these policy recommendations. Although there was no clear evidence to suggest that adding isoniazid would provide additional benefit to this regimen, the 4-drug (H)REZ fixed-dose combination (FDC) may be more convenient for both patients and healthcare services, as it eliminates the need for single-drug formulations. Consistent with the overall framework for managing patients with DR-TB, careful patient selection is a fundamental principle. Before initiating the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen, it is essential to exclude resistance to rifampicin using WHO-recommended genotypic or phenotypic methods. Preferably, resistance to fluoroquinolones and, if possible, pyrazinamide should also be excluded to prevent the acquisition of additional drug resistance. Empirical treatment of Hr-TB is generally not advised. However, in cases where Hr-TB is suspected (e.g., close contacts of Hr-TB cases with active TB but without laboratory confirmation of Hr-TB), the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen may be initiated pending laboratory confirmation of isoniazid resistance, provided rifampicin resistance has been reliably excluded. If DST results later indicate susceptibility to isoniazid, levofloxacin is discontinued, and the patient completes a 2HREZ/4HR regimen. For patients in whom Hr-TB is detected after starting treatment with the 2HREZ/4HR regimen, the (H)REZ component drugs are continued (or pyrazinamide and ethambutol are reintroduced), and levofloxacin is added once rifampicin resistance has been excluded. The duration of the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen is typically determined by the need to complete 6 months of a levofloxacin-containing regimen. In cases where Hr-TB is diagnosed after first-line TB treatment has already begun, the patient may receive more than 6 months of (H)REZ by the end of treatment. Clinicians must decide, based on the patient’s condition, whether to initiate a 6-month course of (H)REZ-levofloxacin at that point. The addition of levofloxacin to (H)REZ is recommended for all patients with Hr-TB, except in the following situations: (i) when resistance to rifampicin cannot be excluded; (ii) known or suspected resistance to levofloxacin; (iii) known intolerance to fluoroquinolones; (iv) known or suspected risk for prolonged QTc interval; and (v) pregnancy or breastfeeding (not an absolute contraindication). In Hr-TB cases where a fluoroquinolone cannot be used, the patient may still be treated with 6(H)REZ. When additional resistance (especially to pyrazinamide) is suspected or confirmed, appropriate treatment regimens must be designed on an individual basis. The reviewed data did not provide separate evidence-based recommendations for such cases. Where possible, isoniazid resistance testing should include information on specific mutations associated with resistance (katG or inhA). Additionally, knowledge of overall host acetylator status at the country or regional level may be useful, as this may have implications for regimen design. High-throughput diagnostic platforms are being developed as an alternative to line probe assays (LPA), which can simultaneously detect TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. Evaluation studies of these diagnostics are ongoing. In the IPD review, only 2% of Hr-TB patients were children, making it impossible to provide a separate estimate of effect for pediatric patients. However, there is no reason why the results and recommendations cannot be extrapolated from adults to children, given that the regimen components have been standard pediatric TB medicines for many years. For patients with extensive disease, although the IPD analysis did not provide evidence for extending treatment duration, prolongation of the 6(H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen beyond 6 months could be considered on an individual basis for patients with extensive disease, as determined by the presence of cavitary disease and persistence of bacteriologically positive sputum at or after month 3. Prolongation of treatment may increase the risk of adverse events in some cases. For HIV-positive individuals, the effect of longer-duration TB treatment among those with and without antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been studied in drug-susceptible TB patients. Relapse rates were four times higher in HIV-infected patients not on ART who received 6 months of treatment compared to those whose treatment was extended to 9 months. In patients with drug-susceptible TB initiated on ART, no significant benefit from prolonging rifampicin-containing regimens beyond 6 months has been observed. In the current analysis, only a limited number of patients received ART. Nonetheless, in TB patients with HIV co-infection, the first priority is to ensure that they are started on ART within 8 weeks of TB treatment initiation, in accordance with WHO guidelines. The 6-month (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen is therefore recommended in HIV-positive patients. For patients with extrapulmonary disease, no data were available for those with exclusive extrapulmonary Hr-TB. However, the proposed regimen composition is likely to be effective even in these patients. Treatment for patients with extrapulmonary TB should be designed in close consultation with appropriate specialists, such as infectious disease physicians and neurologists, to decide on individual variations in treatment duration and supportive care as needed. The implementation of these recommendations requires that the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen is administered only in patients with confirmed isoniazid resistance and excluded rifampicin resistance. Preferably, testing for resistance to fluoroquinolones and, if possible, pyrazinamide, is also conducted before starting treatment. Rapid molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF and LPAs are preferred to guide patient selection for the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen. Surveillance data indicate that fluoroquinolone resistance among patients with rifampicin-susceptible TB is generally low worldwide. However, national data on the prevalence of fluoroquinolone resistance, including targeted or whole-genome sequencing to detect specific mutations, could help guide testing policies when implementing Hr-TB treatment recommendations in countries. Levofloxacin is proposed as the fluoroquinolone of first choice in the Hr-TB treatment regimen for several reasons. Firstly, it has a better-characterized safety profile compared to other fluoroquinolones and was the most frequently used in the studies reviewed for this guidance. Secondly, levofloxacin has fewer known drug interactions with other medications compared to moxifloxacin. For example, while plasma peak concentration and exposure to moxifloxacin decrease significantly when combined with rifampicin, the same effect has not been reported for levofloxacin, which is attributed to its limited metabolism in humans and excretion unchanged in the urine. Additionally, although it may interfere with lamivudine clearance, unlike moxifloxacin, there are no contraindications for its use with other antiretroviral agents.
